::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**In this chapter.** We turn from theories of fertility to real policy changes.
This chapter looks at China's one-child policy, perhaps the most ambitious attempt
by any government to control births, and asks the hard question it shares with the
next chapter: how can we tell what a policy *caused*, when so much else was changing
at the same time?

**Readings this chapter draws on.** Hesketh, Lu, and Xing (2005), "The Effect
of China's One-Child Family Policy after 25 Years"; Zhang (2017), "The Evolution
of China's One-Child Policy and Its Effects on Family Outcomes."
:::

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · new]{.tag-new} Bridge text written for the chapter split.
:::

This is the first of two chapters on fertility policy. Both ask what a policy
change did to births, and both face the same problem of finding a counterfactual.
This chapter takes up China's one-child policy; @sec-abortion turns to abortion and
the pill in the United States.

## Policy and fertility: did it matter, and how would we know?

In earlier chapters we studied *theories* of fertility decline. Now we look at
two cases (this chapter and @sec-abortion) where governments or courts deliberately changed the rules, and ask
what happened to births. Both cases are controversial, and both are useful for the
same reason: they force us to think carefully about **causation**.

The problem is simple to state. Fertility was falling in China before the
one-child policy, and it was falling in the United States before *Roe v. Wade*.
If births fell after a policy, did the policy cause the fall, or would it have
happened anyway? To answer, we need a **counterfactual**: what *would* have
happened without the policy. We can never observe it directly. The art is in
finding a comparison that stands in for it.

Speed of decline is one place to start. Across the world, the time it took
fertility to fall from more than 6 children per woman to fewer than 3 has shrunk
dramatically. In the United Kingdom it took 95 years (1815–1910). In the United
States it took 82 years. In China it took 11 years (1967–1978), and in Iran only
10 (1986–1996). Notice China's dates: its fall from 6 to 3 children per woman was
*finished* before the one-child policy began in 1979. And Iran achieved an even
faster decline with no one-child policy at all.

## The one-child policy: beginnings and end

### Before the one-child policy: "Later, Longer, Fewer"

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · from readings]{.tag-reading} Mao's views, Ma Yinchu, the 1971 slogan,
and the "menstrual monitors" quotation are from Zhang 2017, pp. 142–143.
:::

China's population policy did not begin in 1979. Mao Zedong, China's leader from
1949 to 1976, "believed in the principle: 'More people, more power,'" as Junsen
Zhang puts it. In the mid-1950s the economist Ma Yinchu, president of Peking
University, recommended family planning. Mao was briefly supportive, but during
the Great Leap Forward (1958) he reverted to the belief that a larger population
was better, and Ma was denounced as a "rightist." After the famine of the Great
Leap Forward, fertility rebounded to more than six births per woman in the early
1960s.

By the end of the 1960s, China's population passed 800 million and the economy
was stagnating. A serious family planning campaign began in 1971 with the slogan
"One child isn't too few, two are just fine, and three are too many." In 1973 it
was formalized as the **Later–Longer–Fewer** campaign (*wan–xi–shao*):

- **Later marriage.** People were encouraged to marry three years after the legal
  minimum ages: at least 25 (rural) or 27–28 (urban) for men, and at least 23
  (rural) or 25 (urban) for women. Couples who married late got 7 to 30 days of
  "late marriage leave."
- **Longer spacing.** At least four years between births.
- **Fewer children.** No more than two per couple.

The campaign worked. China's fertility fell by half during the 1970s. Hesketh and
colleagues put the total fertility rate (TFR) at 5.9 in 1970 and 2.9 in 1979;
Zhang gives 5.8 in 1970 and 2.7 in 1978. By 1978, Zhang reports, urban fertility
was already down to 1.55 children per woman, and rural fertility to 2.97.

The campaign was officially voluntary, but it had coercive elements. Zhang quotes
the sociologists Martin Whyte, Wang Feng, and Yong Cai:

> "These birth planning enforcers kept detailed records on each woman of
> child-bearing age under their responsibility, including past births,
> contraceptive usage and even menstrual cycles, in many reported instances
> becoming 'menstrual monitors' who tried to detect out-of-quota pregnancies at an
> early stage."

Still, Zhang concludes, the 1970s campaign was "significantly less coercive than
the one-child policy that followed."

### From Later–Longer–Fewer to just one child

When Deng Xiaoping came to power in 1978, the new leadership's priority was the
economy. A group of control theorists argued that China would achieve the highest
level of well-being around 2050 if its population could be reduced to 650–700
million. Local governments began moving toward a one-child rule in late 1979. The
policy was formally announced in September 1980, in "An open letter to all party
members and all youth league members" published in the *People's Daily*. The
letter said that the State Council "advocates that each couple should have only
one child," and promised that after 30 years the policy might be changed.

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · from readings]{.tag-reading} Hesketh et al. 2005, p. 1171; Zhang 2017,
p. 144.
:::

Hesketh and colleagues summarize the government's reasoning:

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## In their own words
"At the time, China was home to a quarter of the world's people, who were
occupying just 7 percent of world's arable land. Two thirds of the population were
under the age of 30 years, and the baby boomers of the 1950s and 1960s were
entering their reproductive years. The government saw strict population
containment as essential to economic reform and to an improvement in living
standards." (Hesketh, Lu, and Xing 2005)
:::

Zhang adds that Deng had set a goal of quadrupling GDP per capita by the end of
the century. Fewer people was one way to raise income *per person*. The policy was
launched, Zhang writes, "in the context of both a neo-Malthusian concern over
population and ambitious economic development goals."

### How the policy actually worked

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · from readings]{.tag-reading} Details of enforcement are from Hesketh et
al. 2005, pp. 1171–1172, and Zhang 2017, pp. 144–145, including footnote 2.
:::

The name "one-child policy" is misleading. "Despite its name," Hesketh and
colleagues write, "the one-child rule applies to a minority of the population."
In practice there was a two-tier system:

- **Urban residents and government employees** were held strictly to one child.
  Many worked for state-owned enterprises and could lose their jobs and benefits
  if they had a second.
- **Rural residents**, about 70 percent of the population, were generally allowed
  a second child after five years, often only if the first was a girl, "a clear
  acknowledgment of the traditional preference for boys." Ethnic minorities and
  remote areas could have a third.

Enforcement was in the hands of local officials, who used rewards and penalties:
economic incentives for compliance, and fines, confiscation of belongings, and
dismissal from work for violations. The policy relied on near-universal
contraception and abortion. By the early 2000s, 87 percent of married women used
contraception, and IUDs and sterilization made up more than 90 percent of methods.
Eighty percent of women in one large study said they had no choice of method and
simply accepted what the family-planning worker recommended. Zhang notes that the
heavy-handedness peaked in 1983, with "a nationwide campaign of mandatory
sterilization, abortion, and IUD insertion."

The policy also changed over time:

- **Flexibility and decentralization (1984–1989).** Because of "practical
  difficulties," especially resistance from rural families whose only child was a
  girl, the Party allowed more exceptions. The guiding phrase was "open a small hole
  to close up a big one." Fertility rebounded somewhat in 1984–1986.
- **Restrengthening (from 1989).** The policy was tightened again and tied to the
  careers of local officials: "No achievements, no promotion." Family planning was
  listed among the three basic state policies in the 8th Five-Year Plan in March
  1991.

The fines varied enormously from province to province and over time, as you can
see in the data economists have collected on them. That variation will turn out to
be useful for research.

### The end of the one-child policy

The policy was relaxed in steps:

- **1984–2011:** local governments allowed two children for couples in which both
  parents were themselves only children.
- **2014:** two children allowed if *either* parent was an only child.
- **2016:** a universal two-child policy. The abolition of the one-child policy was
  announced on October 29, 2015.
- **2021:** a three-child policy, which lifted limits on third births.

Official motivations for the switch included a lower population growth rate, the
recent decline in the size of the labor force, the challenges of an aging society,
a lasting imbalance in the sex ratio, and the promise made in the 1979 open letter.
Official propaganda has turned around completely. Banners that once read "Strictly
limit second births, totally eradicate third births" and "One child is best, the
government aids in elder care" now read "Three children are better than two" and
"Three children are best, no need for state-supported elder care."

## Did the one-child policy reduce fertility?

### The mystery: where is the policy hiding?

@fig-china-tfr plots the total fertility rates reported in our two readings. The
shaded bands show the Later–Longer–Fewer campaign and the one-child policy.

```{r}
#| label: fig-china-tfr
#| fig-cap: "China's total fertility rate at dates reported in the readings. Black: national; blue and red: urban and rural in 1978. The steepest decline came during the 'Later–Longer–Fewer' campaign of the 1970s, before the one-child policy. Sources: Zhang (2017) for 1970, 1978, 1979, 1995 and the 1978 urban/rural rates; Hesketh et al. (2005) for 2004; Wang, Cai, and Gu (2013), as quoted by Zhang, for 'around 1.5' in 2010."
#| fig-height: 4.2
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(1965, 2015), ylim = c(0, 6.5), xlab = "Year",
     ylab = "Total fertility rate (children per woman)")
rect(1971, -1, 1979, 7, col = adjustcolor("#e08a00", 0.15), border = NA)
rect(1979, -1, 2015.5, 7, col = adjustcolor(col_grey, 0.12), border = NA)
text(1975, 6.3, "Later–Longer–\nFewer", cex = 0.8, col = "#a05a00")
text(1997, 6.3, "One-child policy (1979–2015)", cex = 0.8, col = col_grey)
abline(h = 2.1, lty = 3, col = col_grey)
text(2013.5, 2.1, "replacement", pos = 3, cex = 0.75, col = col_grey)
yr <- c(1970, 1978, 1979, 1995, 2004, 2010)
tfr <- c(5.8, 2.7, 2.8, 1.8, 1.7, 1.5)
lines(yr, tfr, lty = 2, col = col_all)
points(yr, tfr, pch = 19, col = col_all)
text(yr, tfr, c("5.8", "2.7", "2.8", "1.8", "1.7", "~1.5"),
     pos = c(4, 1, 4, 3, 3, 1), cex = 0.8)
points(c(1978, 1978), c(1.55, 2.97), pch = c(17, 15), col = c(col_urban, col_rural))
text(1978, 1.55, "urban 1.55", pos = 2, cex = 0.8, col = col_urban)
text(1978, 2.97, "rural 2.97", pos = 2, cex = 0.8, col = col_rural)
par(op)
```

If you were shown only the curve and asked to find the year the one-child policy
began, it would be hard to pick it out. The big drop came in the 1970s.
Afterward, fertility fell much more gradually, to around 1.8 by the mid-1990s, and
then roughly stabilized. Zhang puts the numbers side by side: the TFR fell from 5.8
to 2.7 between 1970 and 1978, but from 2.8 to 1.8 between 1979 and 1995 under the
one-child policy. Whyte, Wang, and Cai calculate that roughly three-quarters of the
decline in fertility from 1970 to the present occurred *before* the one-child
policy began.

### Comparison countries

Of course, fertility might have *risen* after 1979 without the policy. So we need
a comparison. Zhang compares rural and urban China with four other developing
countries that also had high fertility in the 1960s: South Korea, Thailand, Mexico,
and India. None had a one-child policy. All saw rapid declines after 1970.

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · from readings]{.tag-reading} Zhang 2017, pp. 146–148.
:::

South Korea and Thailand, which had fast economic growth and voluntary family
planning programs, fell more slowly than urban China in the 1960s and 1970s, but by
2010 their fertility was as low as China's. Thailand, Zhang notes, "is especially
worth noting because it had fertility and GDP per capita similar to China's by
2010." Even India, with a weaker family planning program and much slower growth,
saw a marked decline. Zhang's conclusion: "Given that the economic growth rate of
China was higher than those of the four other countries from 1979, I believe that
even without the one-child policy, China's fertility rate would have declined
substantially after 1978."

Another comparison, shown in lecture, is **Taiwan**, which never had a one-child
policy. Taiwan's fertility followed a path quite similar to mainland China's and
has since fallen even lower.

A related observation: China was "ahead of the curve." When we plot fertility
against GDP per capita, China's fertility fell to low levels at an exceptionally
low income. Zhang points out that in China, India, South Korea, and Thailand
fertility fell sharply before GDP per capita reached $3,000. China's economy was
nearly stagnant in the 1970s, so economic development cannot explain the fertility
decline of that decade. The family planning campaign was "widely believed to be the
main contributor." Some demographers called it an "induced fertility transition."

### How economists try to identify the effect

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · from readings]{.tag-reading} The four approaches and their assumptions
are from Zhang 2017, pp. 148–150.
:::

Zhang describes four strategies that researchers have used, each with its own
assumption:

1. **Before and after 1979.** Compare births before and after the policy,
   controlling for a time trend. This assumes that any break from the trend after
   1979 is due to the policy, not to the economic reforms that began at the same
   time.
2. **Variation in fines.** Compare places with higher and lower penalties. The
   problem is that local governments may set fines according to local conditions
   and local demand for children. Fines are not randomly assigned.
3. **Han versus minorities.** Han Chinese women were held strictly to the policy,
   while minority women were often allowed two children. Comparing the change in
   Han fertility to the change in minority fertility is a
   **difference-in-differences** design. It assumes the two groups would otherwise
   have followed the same trend, which economic reforms may have violated.
4. **Variation in enforcement intensity.** Compare prefectures that enforced the
   policy more and less strictly (measured by "excess" births above the one-child
   rule), and cohorts with more and less exposure.

The ideal, Zhang observes wryly, "would have been useful for research purposes if
China had randomly selected a cross-section of prefectures to implement the
one-child policy and then forbidden interprefecture migration." That never
happened, so every estimate rests on assumptions.

### What the evidence says

The studies agree that the policy *did* reduce fertility, especially at first.
Ahn (1994), for example, found that the probability of a second child in urban
areas fell by 50 percent in Hebei and Shaanxi and by 86 percent in Shanghai after
the policy. But most studies find the effect was "rather small, especially in the
longer-term." Zhang offers a reconciliation:

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## In their own words
"A plausible reconciliation of these views is that the one-child policy
accelerated the already-occurring drop in fertility for a few years, but in the
longer term, economic development played a more fundamental role in leading to
and maintaining China's low fertility level." (Zhang 2017)
:::

Hesketh and colleagues reach the same view. China's neighbors, without such
policies, had some of the lowest fertility rates in the world: 1.04 in Singapore,
1.38 in Japan, 0.91 in Hong Kong. "It is reasonable to speculate," they write,
"that there would have been a further decline in China's total fertility rate had
the voluntary policy of the 1970s continued." A Bayesian projection by Wang, Cai,
and Gu, quoted by Zhang, concluded that without the policy, "By 2010, fertility
would have fallen to its currently observed level of around 1.5 children per
woman."

That raises an awkward point about official claims. Chinese authorities claimed
the policy prevented 250 to 300 million births. But that claim depends on assuming
fertility would have stayed high without the policy. Wang and colleagues concluded,
in Zhang's summary, that "China's government exaggerated the effect of the one-child
policy."

### Fewer children, better educated children?

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · from readings]{.tag-reading} Zhang 2017, pp. 152–153.
:::

If families can have only one child, they might invest more in that child. This is
the *quantity–quality trade-off* from Gary Becker's theory of fertility. Did the
one-child policy produce better-educated children?

An ingenious test uses **twins**. In urban Kunming, where the policy was strictly
enforced, about 95 percent of households without twins had one child, while
households whose first birth was twins necessarily had two. Twins are a matter of
chance, so comparing these families isolates the effect of an extra child. Mark
Rosenzweig and Zhang found that the policy-induced fall in fertility had "a
moderately positive effect on children's human capital at most": it raised
schooling by at most 4 percent and the probability of attending college by less
than 9 percent. Other studies, using variation in enforcement, find similarly small
effects on education.

### What lessons for other countries?

Zhang's verdict on the policy as a whole is blunt. It "may have mildly accelerated
the fertility transition," but "it also brought substantial costs, including
political costs, human rights concerns, a more rapidly aging population, and an
imbalanced sex ratio resulting from a preference for sons. In retrospect, one may
question the need for introducing the one-child policy in China." For other
countries:

> "If the country is already experiencing a decline in fertility rates, then a
> one-child policy doesn't seem useful. … Rather than focusing on a one-child
> policy, a developing country may want to consider an aggressive but less-coercive
> family planning program such as the policy implemented in China in the 1970s."
> (Zhang 2017)

## Fewer daughters: an unintended consequence?

### The sex ratio at birth

In every population, slightly more boys are born than girls. Hesketh and colleagues
report that the sex ratio at birth ranges from 1.03 to 1.07 boys per girl in
industrialized countries. In China, the reported ratio rose from 1.06 in 1979 to
1.11 in 1988 and 1.17 in 2001, and reached 1.3 in some rural provinces.
@fig-china-sexratio shows how the ratio varied by birth order.

```{r}
#| label: fig-china-sexratio
#| fig-cap: "Sex ratio at birth (boys per girl) by birth order in China, 1980–2001, for urban and rural areas. The dotted line marks a typical biological ratio of 1.05. Source: Hesketh et al. (2005), Table 2 (data from Kang and Wang)."
#| fig-height: 4
sr <- rbind(Urban = c(1.13, 1.30, 1.19, 1.19), Rural = c(1.05, 1.23, 1.29, 1.32))
colnames(sr) <- c("1st", "2nd", "3rd", "4th+")
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 1, 1))
bp <- barplot(sr, beside = TRUE, col = c(col_urban, col_rural), ylim = c(0.9, 1.4),
              xpd = FALSE, xlab = "Birth order", ylab = "Boys per girl",
              legend.text = TRUE, args.legend = list(x = "topleft", bty = "n"))
abline(h = 1.05, lty = 3, col = col_grey)
box()
text(bp, sr + 0.012, format(sr, nsmall = 2), cex = 0.75)
par(op)
```

The pattern fits the policy's rules closely. In rural areas, where a second child
was usually allowed (especially after a girl), the first-birth ratio was normal,
1.05, but it rose steeply for later births. In urban areas, where only one child
was allowed, the ratio was already high, 1.13, for first births. Hesketh and
colleagues explain:

> "The picture that emerges is that some urban Chinese make the choice to perform
> sex selection with the first pregnancy, since they are allowed only one child. In
> rural areas, most couples are permitted to have a second child, especially if the
> first is female. So if the second (or subsequent) child is female, the pregnancy
> often 'disappears,' allowing the couple to have another child in an attempt to
> have a son."

### Stopping rules can't change the sex ratio. Behavior can.

Could parents raise the share of boys simply by deciding *when to stop* having
children? For example, "keep having children until you get a boy." In class we
test this with coins. The lesson: **stopping rules alone can't change the sex
ratio.** Each birth is still about as likely to be a boy as a girl, whatever the
parents plan to do next. Stopping rules can, however, amplify gender inequality in
other ways. (Think about how many brothers and sisters a typical boy or girl has
under such a rule.)

So if we see the sex ratio change, it must be due to **behavior** that affects
which births are born or counted:

- **sex-selective abortion**, made possible by ultrasound;
- **differential reporting**, or "hiding girls" from census takers and officials;
- **differential mortality**, if girls receive less care;
- and possibly other channels.

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · from readings]{.tag-reading} Hesketh et al. 2005, pp. 1172–1173; Zhang
2017, pp. 153–154.
:::

The readings suggest that all three behaviors played a role. Sex-selective abortion
"undoubtedly accounts for a large proportion of the decline in female births,"
Hesketh and colleagues write, although it is illegal and hard to measure.
Underreporting was large too. A 1995 household survey in three provinces found a
normal sex ratio among children under 14, with the actual number of girls exceeding
the number *registered* by 22 percent. Daniel Goodkind estimated that 19 percent of
all children aged 0–4 in 2000 were unreported to the authorities. Infanticide of
girls is "probably very rare now," but "less aggressive treatment of sick female
infants is known to occur."

Was the policy itself to blame? Only partly, say Hesketh and colleagues. China had
a high sex ratio in the 1930s and 1940s, and other Asian countries with son
preference and falling fertility, but no one-child policy, also saw imbalances:
Taiwan (1.19), Singapore (1.18), South Korea (1.12), and parts of northern India
(1.20). Most tellingly, "the marked increase in the sex ratio between the 1980s and
1990s coincided with much easier access to cheap ultrasonography and not with any
substantial change in enforcement of the one-child policy." The policy amplified son
preference, but technology made acting on it easy.

### Other consequences

Hesketh and colleagues list several more consequences:

- **A marriage squeeze.** The shortage of women has left some men unable to marry.
  The authors link it to the kidnapping and trafficking of women for marriage.
- **The "4:2:1" problem.** With few children and longer lives, a growing number of
  couples will be solely responsible for one child and four parents. About 70
  percent of elderly people still depended financially on their children.
- **Health risks.** Women with unapproved pregnancies often avoided prenatal care
  and gave birth at home. One study found that maternal deaths doubled for
  unapproved pregnancies.

::: {.callout-important}
## In the lab
In Lab 8 you use a sample of the 1990 Chinese census, about 200,000
households, to look for traces of the one-child policy in the sexes of children.
You compare the proportion female by birth order and year of birth, and you ask
whether parents' decisions to have another child depended on the sexes of the
children they already had. Keep in mind that the 1990 census is known to undercount
young children, and that we see only surviving children.
:::

## Key ideas

- To know what a policy *caused*, we need a **counterfactual**. Comparison countries,
  comparison groups, and natural experiments stand in for it.
- China's fertility fell by half during the voluntary but coercive **Later–Longer–Fewer**
  campaign of the 1970s, *before* the one-child policy. The policy itself seems to have
  had a modest, mostly short-term effect.
- China's **sex ratio at birth** rose sharply, especially for later births in rural
  areas and first births in cities. Stopping rules cannot change the sex ratio;
  sex-selective abortion, underreporting, and differential care can.

## Check your understanding

::: {.column-margin}
[Added · new]{.tag-new} These questions are new. They avoid the China lab's graded
questions on third births and the in-class coin exercise.
:::

1. **Urban versus rural.** In @fig-china-sexratio, the sex ratio for *first* births is
   high in cities but normal in the countryside. Use the rules of the one-child policy
   to explain why.

2. **Twins.** Why does comparing families whose first birth was twins with
   one-child families help identify the effect of family size on children's
   education? Give one reason the comparison might still be imperfect.

3. **Han and minorities.** In the Han-versus-minority difference-in-differences design,
   what is the "common trend" assumption? Give an example of something that might
   violate it.

4. **China and Iran.** Iran's fertility fell from more than 6 to fewer than 3 children
   per woman in about 10 years, with no one-child policy. What does this suggest about
   how much a coercive policy is needed for a rapid fertility decline?

## Further reading

- Hesketh, Therese, Li Lu, and Zhu Wei Xing. 2005. "The Effect of China's One-Child
  Family Policy after 25 Years." *New England Journal of Medicine* 353: 1171–1176.
  *An overview of how the policy worked and its consequences. As you read: Why do the
  authors think the policy is only partly responsible for the fall in fertility, and
  for the rise in the sex ratio?*
- Zhang, Junsen. 2017. "The Evolution of China's One-Child Policy and Its Effects on
  Family Outcomes." *Journal of Economic Perspectives* 31(1): 141–160. *As you read:
  Focus on the four empirical approaches and their assumptions. Which do you find most
  convincing?*
